evidence: src/application/order-service.ts: the constructor injects the ProductRepository and OrderRepository ports and uses no concrete persistence
placeOrder checks input, checks every product first with product.canReserve, then calls product.reserve and the repository save calls (application coordination)
advance calls order.advanceTo(next), so state-transition rules stay in the domain Order; it also coordinates product.consumeReserved across aggregates
cancel calls order.cancel() and product.release(), handing the rules to domain entities
level() maps a Product to the StockLevel read model, a normal application-layer mapping
The file has no HTTP, framework, SQL or storage-specific code
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService is a typical application-layer use-case service. It handles input from callers, loads aggregates through injected repository ports (ProductRepository, OrderRepository), hands state changes to domain methods (Product.reserve, consumeReserved, release, canReserve; Order.advanceTo, cancel), and saves the results. Each method's responsibilities fit the application role: checking input (required fields, positive integer quantities, known state filter), coordinating across aggregates (consuming reserved stock when an order ships, releasing stock on cancel), running a validate-then-reserve sequence so a failed order reserves nothing, and mapping results to a read model (StockLevel). The file contains no persistence code (no SQL or storage access), no transport or framework code (no HTTP or request/response handling), and no presentation logic. Core rules such as the order state flow and stock invariants stay in the domain entities. Two items are borderline: merging duplicate order lines, and the 'shipped triggers consume' rule could arguably sit in the domain. Both are reasonable as cross-aggregate coordination, so neither clearly breaks the layer role. No ADR prose was provided.
